q: Which plane divides the body into right and left parts?
options: Frontal plane
Transverse plane
Sagittal plane
Oblique plane

why.correct: The sagittal plane (sagitta = arrow) is a vertical plane running front to back, so it separates right from left.
options: The frontal plane runs side to side and separates anterior from posterior.
The transverse plane is horizontal and separates superior from inferior.
Correct. Sagittal planes divide right from left.
An oblique plane runs at a slant between the main planes, so it does not cleanly separate right from left.

q: Which plane divides the body into anterior and posterior parts?
options: Frontal plane
Midsagittal plane
Transverse plane
Parasagittal plane

why.correct: The frontal plane, also called the coronal plane, is a vertical plane running from side to side, so it separates front from back.
options: Correct. Frontal (coronal) planes divide anterior from posterior.
The midsagittal plane divides the body into equal right and left halves.
The transverse plane divides superior from inferior.
A parasagittal plane divides the body into unequal right and left parts.

q: A section cuts through the right eye and the right ear but misses the nose. Which plane made it?
options: Midsagittal
Transverse
Parasagittal
Frontal

why.correct: A vertical cut that stays on the right side, off the midline, is parasagittal. It divides the head into unequal right and left parts.
options: A midsagittal cut runs down the exact midline, through the middle of the nose.
A horizontal cut at eye level would pass through both eyes and both ears, not just the right ones.
Correct. Off the midline, dividing right from left unequally: parasagittal.
A frontal cut through the eyes would pass through both eyes, since it runs from side to side.

q: What is another name for the frontal plane?
options: Median plane
Coronal plane
Horizontal plane
Axial plane

why.correct: The frontal plane is also called the coronal plane (corona = crown), because it runs like a headband over the head from ear to ear.
options: The median plane is another name for the midsagittal plane.
Correct. Frontal and coronal name the same plane.
Horizontal is another name for the transverse plane.
Axial is the imaging name for the transverse plane.

q: A pathologist sees a round ring of tissue with a hollow center under the microscope. What is the most likely explanation?
options: A tube cut in cross section
A tube cut in longitudinal section
A solid ball cut through its middle
A flat sheet cut at a slant

why.correct: Cutting a tube straight across its length gives a ring: the wall around a hollow channel.
options: Correct. A tube cut across shows a ring.
A tube cut along its length shows two parallel walls with the channel between them, not a ring.
A solid ball cut through its middle gives a filled disk, with no hollow center.
A flat sheet cut at a slant gives a straight strip, not a closed ring.

q: Select every term that names the transverse plane or its cut.
options: Horizontal plane
Coronal plane
Cross section
Axial plane
Median plane

why.correct: The transverse plane is also called the horizontal plane, imaging staff call it the axial plane, and the section it produces is a cross section.
options: Correct. Horizontal is another name for transverse.
Coronal is another name for the frontal plane.
Correct. A cut along the transverse plane is a cross section.
Correct. Axial is the imaging name for the transverse plane.
Median is another name for the midsagittal plane.

q: What is the difference between a plane and a section?
options: A plane is horizontal; a section is vertical
A plane is an imaginary surface; a section is the cut it produces
A plane is used for single organs; a section is used for the whole body
A plane is seen on a scan; a section is seen only in dissection

why.correct: A plane is an imaginary flat surface that sets a direction. A section is the actual surface you see once the body or an organ is divided along that plane.
options: Planes can be vertical (sagittal, frontal) or horizontal (transverse), and so can sections.
Correct. Plane = imaginary surface; section = the cut surface.
Both terms apply to organs and to the whole body.
Scans show sections too. CT, MRI and ultrasound all produce sections without any cutting.

q: A pregnant patient needs imaging of her gallbladder, and her doctor wants to avoid ionizing radiation. Which method fits best?
options: CT scan
Ultrasound
PET scan
Radiograph

why.correct: Ultrasound makes images from echoes of sound waves and uses no ionizing radiation. The gallbladder is a fluid-filled organ, which ultrasound shows well.
options: CT uses X-rays from many angles, a larger dose of ionizing radiation.
Correct. Sound waves, no ionizing radiation, and good views of fluid-filled organs.
PET uses a radioactive tracer, which exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
A radiograph uses X-rays, which are ionizing radiation.

q: On a radiograph of the forearm, the bones look white and the surrounding soft tissue looks gray. What causes this difference?
options: Bone reflects sound waves back toward the probe on the skin
Bone gives off radio signals in a magnetic field
Bone absorbs more of the X-rays passing through it
Bone takes up more of an injected tracer

why.correct: Dense bone absorbs more X-rays than soft tissue. Fewer rays reach the detector behind the bone, and those areas show as white.
options: Reflected sound waves are how ultrasound works, not radiographs.
Radio signals in a magnetic field are how MRI works.
Correct. More absorption means fewer X-rays reach the detector behind the bone, which shows as white.
Tracer uptake is how PET works. A radiograph uses no tracer.

q: Put the steps of making a CT image in order.
options: An X-ray source spins around the patient, sending beams through from many angles
Detectors record how much each beam was weakened
A computer calculates the density at every point in a thin slice
The densities are shown as shades from black to white in a transverse section
The stack of transverse sections is rebuilt into sagittal or frontal views

why.correct: Beams pass through from many angles; detectors measure how much each is weakened; the computer turns those measurements into the density at each point; the densities become a grayscale transverse section; and a stack of sections can be rebuilt in other planes.

q: On a chest radiograph, a coin in the patient's shirt pocket appears on top of the heart shadow. Why can't the radiograph alone tell whether the coin is in front of or behind the heart?
options: A coin is too small and too faint to show clearly on a radiograph
Radiographs show only soft tissue
The heart blocks all X-rays
Radiographs flatten everything on a beam's path into one image
misconception: a plain X-ray shows a slice

why.correct: A radiograph is a shadow. Everything the beam crosses, front to back, is laid on top of everything else in one flat image, so depth is lost. A second view from the side, or a CT, shows which is in front.
options: Metal absorbs X-rays strongly, so a coin shows clearly as white. The problem is depth, not visibility.
Radiographs show bone and metal best of all. Soft tissue shows only as shades of gray.
X-rays pass through the heart; that is why its outline appears as a gray shadow rather than a solid block.
Correct. Projection, not section: depth is lost.

q: A radiologist reads a transverse CT slice of a patient's abdomen. The liver appears on the left side of the screen. On which side of the patient is the liver?
options: The patient's left
It cannot be known from a CT slice
The patient's right
It depends on whether the patient was prone

why.correct: Transverse CT images are viewed as if you stand at the patient's feet looking toward the head, just as when you face a person. The patient's right appears on the left of the screen. The liver lies on the patient's right.
options: The screen's left is the patient's right, the same as when you face someone.
The viewing convention is fixed, so the side can be read directly from the image.
Correct. Screen left is patient right.
The images are displayed in a standard orientation whatever the position of the patient in the scanner, so right and left still follow the convention.

q: A patient with a metal fragment near the eye needs imaging. Which method is most likely to be unsafe?
options: Radiograph
CT scan
Ultrasound
MRI

why.correct: MRI uses a very strong magnet. It can pull on some metal objects in the body, so a metal fragment near the eye can move and cause injury.
options: A radiograph uses X-rays, which do not move metal. The fragment would simply show up white.
CT uses X-rays too. Metal causes bright streaks on the image but is not moved by the scan.
Ultrasound uses sound waves, which do not move metal fragments.
Correct. The MRI magnet is the hazard.

q: A doctor wants to see which areas of a patient's body contain very active cells, such as an active cancer. Which method shows this best?
options: PET scan
Radiograph
Ultrasound
Midsagittal dissection

why.correct: PET uses an injected tracer that very active cells take up more of, so it maps activity. It is usually combined with CT to place that activity on the anatomy.
options: Correct. PET shows where cells are most active.
A radiograph shows density, mainly bone and air, not how active the cells are.
Ultrasound shows tissue boundaries and movement, not how active the cells are.
Dissection is done on a body after death and shows structure, not living activity.

q: Complete the list. Sagittal divides right from left; frontal divides anterior from posterior; transverse divides ____.
options: Medial from lateral
Superior from inferior
Proximal from distal
Superficial from deep

why.correct: The transverse plane is horizontal, so it separates the upper (superior) part from the lower (inferior) part.
options: Medial and lateral compare distance from the midline; the sagittal plane divides along that direction.
Correct. Transverse separates superior from inferior.
Proximal and distal apply along a limb and are not divided by one standard plane.
Superficial and deep compare distance from the surface, not a direction a main plane divides.

q: A student lists how each imaging method works. One entry is wrong. Find it.
options: Radiograph: X-rays absorbed by dense tissue leave white areas on a flat image
CT: X-rays from many angles are turned into sections by a computer
MRI: X-rays and a radioactive tracer make sections in any plane
Ultrasound: echoes of sound waves make a live section

why.correct: MRI uses a strong magnet and radio waves, not X-rays or a tracer. The magnetic field lines up hydrogen nuclei, radio pulses disturb them, and their returning signals build the image.
options: This entry is right. Dense tissue absorbs more X-rays and appears white on the flat projection.
This entry is right. CT computes sections from many X-ray measurements.
This is the wrong entry. MRI uses a magnet and radio waves; a radioactive tracer belongs to PET.
This entry is right. Ultrasound builds a live section from echoes.
